summary: Defines DRIP message types and formats carried in Broadcast Remote ID Authentication Messages for drones (unmanned aircraft). They let observers verify that the attached messages and the sender are trustworthy, even without Internet access.

plainLanguage.summary: Drones broadcast who they are. This adds a signature so people nearby can check the broadcast is real, even without internet.

questions: what is drone remote id authentication
what is a drip entity tag
subtitle: Signed drone broadcasts that nearby observers can check, even with no Internet connection.

tldr.problem: Broadcast Remote ID messages from drones can say anything, and an observer cannot tell whether they came from the claimed aircraft or from a spoofing transmitter within radio range.
tldr.mechanism: DRIP defines four Specific Authentication Method (SAM) types for the ASTM Authentication Message: Link carries signed Broadcast Endorsements of the DET registration chain, and Wrapper, Manifest and Frame carry data signed by the aircraft with its own key. A simple XOR parity page adds error correction over Bluetooth 4.x.
tldr.outcome: An observer who gathers the endorsement chain and validates signed, nonce-like data such as a Location/Vector Message can trust that the observed aircraft holds the registered key, even when offline.

today: RFC 9575 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves DNS usage and the DET registry hierarchy to a separate Internet-Draft, and no DRIP Frame Types were defined at publication.

sections.title: The Trust Gap in Broadcast Remote ID
sections.content:
Regulations and the ASTM F3411 standard for Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS) Remote Identification (RID) do not address trust. Broadcast RID is a one-way radio transmission of MAC layer messages over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi. Senders can make any claims the message formats allow, and observers cannot verify them, nor detect whether a message came from the aircraft or from a laptop or smartphone within broadcast range.

RFC 9575 is part of the Drone Remote ID Protocol (DRIP). It defines message types and formats, carried in ASTM Authentication Messages (Message Type 0x2) and used with DRIP Entity Tags (DETs), that let an observer verify that attached and recently detached messages were signed by the registered owner of the claimed DET. It also supplies the error correction the US FAA requires and ASTM F3411 lacks over Legacy Transports (Bluetooth 4.x).
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone with a radio can shout 'I am drone number 7'. This document gives real drones a way to prove it, like a signed name tag that is hard to fake.

sections.title: ASTM Framing and Its Limits
sections.content:
ASTM F3411 defines only the framing of Authentication Messages, not the methods. DRIP uses the third-party slot Authentication Type 0x5, the Specific Authentication Method (SAM), and the first octet of the authentication data (the SAM Type) says which format follows.

An Authentication Message is split into pages: a 1-octet header (4-bit type, 4-bit page number) and a 23-octet payload. At most 16 pages (0 to 15) are possible. Over Legacy Transports (Bluetooth 4.x) each page goes in its own frame of 25 octets. Extended Transports (Bluetooth 5.x, Wi-Fi NAN, IEEE 802.11 Beacon) put everything in one Message Pack (Message Type 0xF).

To work on the most constrained transport, Bluetooth 5.x at 9 pages, DRIP data must fit in pages 0 to 8, and the Authentication Headers Length field must not exceed 201. Timestamps count from 2019-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. Each structure carries Valid Not Before (VNB) and Valid Not After (VNA) timestamps, and for UA signatures the RFC suggests VNA about 2 minutes after VNB.
sections.plainLanguage: A long message is cut into small postcards that are sent one by one. The radio only fits a tiny card in each go, so everything has to be packed carefully.

sections.title: How an Observer Builds Trust
sections.content:
Two things together give trust. First, the aircraft broadcasts a chain of Broadcast Endorsements (BEs), each made by a DRIP Identity Management Entity (DIME) for its child. The chain runs from the DET prefix owner down to the individual UA registration. This proves the DET and its public key (Host Identity, HI) are registered, but replay is trivial, so it does not prove the sender holds the key.

Second, the UA proves possession of the private key by signing data that is unique and unpredictable but easy for the observer to check. The observer must verify the signature and then validate the content by non-cryptographic means, such as comparing a signed location with where the aircraft is seen. Observers MUST validate all signatures. A missing HI comes from a pre-configured cache, received endorsements or DNS lookups, and an observer MUST query DNS when connectivity allows. Whether the content is true is a separate question DRIP cannot answer.
sections.plainLanguage: First you check the school's stamp on the student's ID card. Then you ask the student a quick question only the real owner could answer. Both checks together make you trust them.

sections.title: DRIP Link and UA-Signed Evidence
sections.content:
DRIP Link (SAM Type 0x01) carries one Broadcast Endorsement: the parent's VNB and VNA timestamps, the child's DET (16 octets) and HI (32 octets), the parent's DET (16 octets) and the parent's 64-octet signature over those fields. The endorsement proving a DET is registered MUST come from its immediate parent, for example an HHIT Domain Authority (HDA) for a UA. Verifying a Link needs no Internet access when the DIME's DET and HI are cached.

The UA-Signed Evidence Structure is used by Wrapper, Manifest and Frame, but not by Link. It holds VNB and VNA set by the UA, 0 to 112 octets of Evidence, the 16-octet UA DET and a 64-octet UA signature over the preceding fields, made with the key pair of the DET. The signature algorithm comes from the Suite ID in the DET.
sections.plainLanguage: A Link is a note from a parent saying 'this child is really mine'. The signed evidence is the child adding a fresh signature of their own on top.

sections.title: Wrapper, Manifest and Frame
sections.content:
DRIP Wrapper (0x02) puts up to four ASTM messages, in Message Type order, into the Evidence field and signs them. Only Message Types 0x0, 0x1, 0x3, 0x4 and 0x5 are allowed, each 25 octets without the Message Counter octet. On Extended Transports the Evidence can be left out of the Authentication Message, because the receiver rebuilds it from the other messages in the Message Pack. Wrapped data is sent twice, once in the clear and once inside the Wrapper, since a non-DRIP observer still needs the plain message.

DRIP Manifest (0x03) signs 8-octet hashes of previously sent messages: up to 11, with 10 recommended. Three special hashes always come first: the previous Manifest hash, the current Manifest hash and a hash of the Link carrying BE: HDA, UA. The first Manifest uses a random nonce as the previous hash. The hash uses the algorithm of the signing DET; for cSHAKE128 it is cSHAKE128(ASTM Message, 64, "", "Remote ID Auth Hash"). At least one hashed message must be nonce-like data, tying the endorsement to fresh content.

DRIP Frame (0x04) reserves room for future formats: one Frame Type octet plus up to 111 octets of data. In 2024 no Frame Types are defined, only an Experimental range.
sections.plainLanguage: A Wrapper is signing the whole photo. A Manifest is signing a list of tiny fingerprints of many photos you already sent, which takes much less space. A Frame is an empty envelope kept for later ideas.

sections.title: Forward Error Correction
sections.content:
Bluetooth 4.x detects errors but cannot correct them, so a damaged frame is simply dropped. DRIP treats this as an erasure and adds a single-page FEC based on XOR parity over the 23-octet payloads of all pages. It can restore one lost page; if more are missing, higher layers decide what to do with the incomplete message. FEC MUST be used on media without FEC, such as Bluetooth 4.x.

The parity goes in the Additional Data field, outside the signed data, and must start on a new page, so the Last Page Index is increased accordingly. Padding of nulls aligns it, and the Additional Data Length covers padding plus parity. A receiver detects FEC when Last Page Index is one greater than the authentication data needs. If Page 0 is rebuilt, the Last Page Index and Length must be checked. In the worst case a whole page is wasted just to carry the Additional Data Length. Message Packs never use DRIP FEC, because their transports already have it.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a puzzle with one extra piece that is a clever sum of all the others. If one piece goes missing, the sum lets you work out what it looked like.

sections.title: Sending Schedule and Observer Duties
sections.content:
To meet the DRIP requirements of RFC 9153, a UA MUST send:

  • a Link with BE: Apex, RAA at least once per 5 minutes;
  • a Link with BE: RAA, HDA at least once per 5 minutes;
  • a Link with BE: HDA, UA at least once per minute;
  • a non-Link format, signing unique and unpredictable data that is easy to check, at least once per 5 seconds.

The observer must verify the signature on each of these and validate the signed content of the last, non-Link message. Over Legacy Transports, messages with dynamic data may be sent at least every 1 second. The RFC's example schedule for Legacy Transports sends the messages regulators require twice per second plus a Manifest, and spreads the Link over 8 seconds; a full endorsement chain is received within 136 seconds.

Wrappers must be sent in addition to, never in place of, required ASTM messages. If the correlation of observed data fails thresholds, the data must be rejected as if the signature had failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The drone must show its family tree every so often and show a fresh signature every few seconds, so a watcher always has recent proof.

sections.title: Replay Attacks and Wrapper vs Manifest
sections.content:
ASTM F3411 has no replay protection, so an attacker can copy a sender's address and ID and replay genuine messages. A valid signature alone is not enough. Trust that the sender holds the private key comes only when a Wrapper or Manifest signature checks out, the signed content is nonce-like (unique, changing, hard to predict, easy to validate) and the observer validates it by other means, for example a Location/Vector Message matched with the visible aircraft. Replay of static messages such as Basic ID or Operator ID stays a risk unless combined with nonce-like data in a Wrapper or Manifest. Replaying Link messages is harmless.

The RFC compares the two formats. Wrapper authenticates full content but cannot bind to the trust chain. Manifest binds to the last Link and covers more messages (11 versus 4), at the cost of the observer storing and comparing hashes. In its example, the totals are 36 frames with Wrappers versus 25 with a Manifest. For UA signatures, VNA offset of 3 to 5 minutes is recommended. DNS security options are left to another document.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed photo of yesterday's weather proves nothing about today. So the signed thing has to be fresh, like today's time on a clock you can see yourself.
